{{DISPLAYTITLE:Structural and well-founded recursion}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Functions that always finish|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Induction, as the machine sees it}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Lean lets a function be defined by calling itself, but Lean's kernel knows nothing of
recursive definitions. Before a recursive definition reaches the Lean kernel, the elaborator
replaces the recursion by a non-recursive term built from recursors or from a well-founded
fixed-point combinator, and the fact that this translation succeeds is the proof that the
function terminates. This page explains why unrestricted recursion is not allowed, how
'''structural recursion''' is compiled through the recursor, how '''well-founded recursion'''
is compiled through <code>WellFounded.fix</code>, what <code>termination_by</code> and
<code>decreasing_by</code> control, how <code>partial</code> and <code>unsafe</code>
definitions are kept from compromising the logic, and the induction principles Lean derives from a
recursive definition.

== Why recursion must be checked ==

If any recursive equation were accepted as a definition, the logic would be inconsistent. The
equation <code>f n = f n + 1</code> would define a natural-number function with the absurd
property that a number equals its successor; and a function into the empty type
<code>Empty</code> that simply calls itself would produce an element of a type with no
elements, from which anything follows. A proof that "P holds because P holds" would be
accepted.<ref name="refman-rec">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0,
lean-lang.org, 2026, section 7.6, "Recursive Definitions".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/</ref> Lean's
logic therefore treats every function as '''total''': defined on every argument and
returning in finitely many steps.<ref name="refman-fn">''The Lean Language Reference'', for
Lean 4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, section 4.1, "Functions".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Functions/</ref>

Termination is not checked by Lean's kernel, which has no termination checker; it is
guaranteed because every recursive function is elaborated into uses of primitive
recursors, which cannot loop.<ref name="refman-elab">''The Lean Language Reference'', for
Lean 4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, sections 2.3, "The Kernel", and 2.4, "Elaboration
Results". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/</ref>
Elaboration proceeds in two phases. First the definition is elaborated as if the core
language had recursion, giving a '''pre-definition'''; the compiler generates code from
it unchanged. Then a termination analysis translates the pre-definition into a non-recursive
term for the Lean kernel. Without an explicit instruction the elaborator tries structural recursion
on each argument in turn, and then searches for a decreasing measure for well-founded
recursion.<ref name="refman-rec" /> The reference manual also describes partial fixpoints and
predicates defined as least or greatest fixed points; this page does not treat them.

== Structural recursion ==

A definition is '''structurally recursive''' when every recursive call is on a strict
sub-term of one fixed argument, the '''decreasing parameter''', as exposed by pattern
matching.<ref name="refman-rec" /> The Fibonacci function is a standard example:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def fib : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 0
  | 1 => 1
  | n + 2 => fib n + fib (n + 1)

#print fib
example : fib 10 = 55 := rfl
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints the term the Lean kernel received:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def fib : Nat → Nat :=
fun x => Nat.brecOn x fib._f
</pre>

There is no self-reference. The recursion has become an application of
<code>Nat.brecOn</code>, and the cases of the definition are in an auxiliary function
<code>fib._f</code>.

<code>fib</code> calls itself on <code>n</code>, two steps below its argument, so the plain
recursor, whose step function sees only the result for the immediate predecessor, does not fit
directly. The elaborator uses two constructions derived from the recursor instead. For a
motive <code>C</code>, <code>Nat.below t</code> is a table holding a value of
<code>C k</code> for every <code>k</code> smaller than <code>t</code>, built as an iterated
pair; <code>Nat.brecOn</code> is a recursor whose step function receives that whole table, so
it can use the result for any smaller argument. This is '''course-of-values recursion'''.
Lean generates <code>below</code> and <code>brecOn</code> for every inductive type, following
McBride, Goguen and McKinna.<ref name="refman-ind">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean
4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, section 4.4.3.3, "Constructions for Termination Checking".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/</ref><ref name="mgm">Conor
McBride, Healfdene Goguen and James McKinna, "A Few Constructions on Constructors", in
''Types for Proofs and Programs'' (TYPES 2004), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 3839,
Springer, 2006, pp. 186–200. https://doi.org/10.1007/11617990_12</ref>

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check @Nat.brecOn
#print fib._f
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
@Nat.brecOn : {motive : Nat → Sort u_1} → (t : Nat) → ((t : Nat) → Nat.below t → motive t) → motive t
@[reducible] def fib._f : (x : Nat) → Nat.below x → Nat :=
fun x f =>
  (match (motive := (x : Nat) → Nat.below x → Nat) x with
    | 0 => fun x => 0
    | 1 => fun x => 1
    | n.succ.succ => fun x => x.2.1 + x.1)
    f
</pre>

In the last case the two recursive calls have become two lookups in the table:
<code>x.1</code> is the entry for <code>n + 1</code> and <code>x.2.1</code> the entry for
<code>n</code>. Because <code>brecOn</code> and <code>below</code> are themselves defined from
<code>Nat.rec</code>, the whole definition reduces by the ordinary rules of definitional
equality, which is why <code>fib 10 = 55</code> holds by <code>rfl</code>. Structurally
recursive functions compute inside Lean's kernel, and their defining equations hold
definitionally.<ref name="refman-elab" />

The analysis is syntactic, so some terminating functions fail it. A function that tests
<code>n == 0</code> and recurses on <code>n - 1</code> terminates, but <code>n - 1</code> is
not exposed as a sub-term by any pattern match, so it is not structural; such functions need
well-founded recursion.<ref name="refman-rec" /> The clause
<code>termination_by structural x</code> names the decreasing parameter explicitly and
forbids the fallback.

The term built from <code>brecOn</code> is not what runs. Compiled code is generated from the
pre-definition with ordinary recursion; the recursor-based term exists to justify
termination, not to be executed.<ref name="refman-elab" /><ref name="refman-ind" />

== Well-founded recursion ==

A relation <math>\prec</math> is '''well-founded''' when there is no infinite descending chain
<math>x_0 \succ x_1 \succ x_2 \succ \cdots</math>. Lean states this through the accessibility
predicate <code>Acc</code>, an inductive proposition: <code>x</code> is accessible when every
<code>y ≺ x</code> is accessible, and a relation is well-founded when every element is
accessible.<ref name="refman-rec" /> A function whose arguments decrease along a well-founded
relation at every recursive call can be defined with the fixed-point combinator

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check @WellFounded.fix
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
@WellFounded.fix : {α : Sort u_1} →
  {C : α → Sort u_2} → {r : α → α → Prop} → WellFounded r → ((x : α) → ((y : α) → r y x → C y) → C x) → (x : α) → C x
</pre>

Its step function receives the current argument <code>x</code> and a function that may be
called only on arguments <code>y</code> accompanied by a proof of <code>r y x</code>.
<code>WellFounded.fix</code> is defined through an auxiliary function,
<code>WellFounded.fixF</code>, that takes the accessibility proof as an explicit argument:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print WellFounded.fixF
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def WellFounded.fixF.{u, v} : {α : Sort u} →
  {r : α → α → Prop} → {C : α → Sort v} → ((x : α) → ((y : α) → r y x → C y) → C x) → (x : α) → Acc r x → C x :=
fun {α} {r} {C} F x a => Acc.rec (fun x₁ h ih => F x₁ ih) a
</pre>

Its body is one application of <code>Acc.rec</code>, the recursor of the accessibility
predicate. Well-founded recursion is therefore structural recursion again, on a proof that
the arguments decrease rather than on the data.<ref name="refman-elab" /> A
function's several arguments are packed into a single dependent pair, the relation is pulled
back from the measure with <code>invImage</code>, and each recursive call is given its proof
of decrease.<ref name="refman-rec" />

The measure is given with '''<code>termination_by</code>''' and the proofs of decrease with
'''<code>decreasing_by</code>''':

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def log2 (n : Nat) : Nat :=
  if h : n &lt; 2 then 0 else 1 + log2 (n / 2)
termination_by n
decreasing_by omega

#eval log2 1024
#print log2
</pre>

The evaluation prints <code>10</code>, and <code>#print</code> shows

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
@[irreducible] def log2 : Nat → Nat :=
WellFounded.Nat.fix (fun x => x) fun n a => if h : n &lt; 2 then 0 else 1 + a (n / 2) ⋯
</pre>

The recursive call <code>log2 (n / 2)</code> has become <code>a (n / 2) ⋯</code>, where
<code>⋯</code> stands for the proof, produced by <code>omega</code>, that
<code>n / 2 &lt; n</code> in the branch where <code>n</code> is at least 2. Here the measure
is a natural number, and since Lean 4.27.0 such definitions use
<code>WellFounded.Nat.fix</code>, a variant whose recursion runs on a natural-number "fuel"
argument initialised from the measure, which makes the definitions easier to
evaluate.<ref name="rel427">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0, lean-lang.org,
2026, release notes, "Lean 4.27.0", section "Language".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/releases/v4.27.0/</ref> For other measures, such
as a pair of numbers compared lexicographically, the elaborator produces a term built on
<code>WellFounded.fix</code> directly. When <code>decreasing_by</code> is omitted a default
tactic tries to prove each obligation.<ref name="refman-rec" />

The <code>@[irreducible]</code> attribute is the visible difference from structural
recursion. Definitions by well-founded recursion are irreducible by default, so the
elaborator will not unfold them while checking definitional equality, and an equation that
would follow by computation is not accepted by <code>rfl</code>:<ref name="refman-rec" />

<pre class="lean lean-cont lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : log2 8 = 3 := rfl
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Type mismatch
  rfl
has type
  ?m.7 = ?m.7
but is expected to have type
  log2 8 = 3
</pre>

The equation is still true, and Lean proves the defining equation as a theorem,
<code>log2.eq_1</code>, so that <code>simp [log2]</code> can rewrite with it and prove the
example. Even when the reductions do hold definitionally, they may be slow in the
Lean kernel, which must unfold the proof of termination along with the definition. The reference
manual's advice is to use structural recursion, where possible, for functions meant for use
in types or wherever definitional equality matters.<ref name="refman-rec" />

== Functional induction ==

A recursive definition determines an induction principle that follows its own case split and
recursive calls. Since Lean 4.8.0 the elaborator derives it automatically, as a theorem named
<code>f.induct</code> for a recursive function <code>f</code>.<ref name="rel48">''The Lean
Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, release notes, "Lean 4.8.0"
(functional induction principles) and "Lean 4.18.0" (the <code>fun_induction</code> tactic).
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/releases/v4.8.0/ and
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/releases/v4.18.0/</ref> It exists for the
structurally recursive <code>fib</code> as well as for the well-founded
<code>log2</code>:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check @fib.induct
#check @log2.induct

theorem log2_le (n : Nat) : log2 n ≤ n := by
  fun_induction log2 n with
  | case1 n h => simp
  | case2 n h ih => omega
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
fib.induct : ∀ (motive : Nat → Prop),
  motive 0 → motive 1 → (∀ (n : Nat), motive n → motive (n + 1) → motive n.succ.succ) → ∀ (a : Nat), motive a
log2.induct : ∀ (motive : Nat → Prop),
  (∀ (x : Nat), x &lt; 2 → motive x) → (∀ (x : Nat), ¬x &lt; 2 → motive (x / 2) → motive x) → ∀ (n : Nat), motive n
</pre>

Each principle has one case for each branch of its function. For <code>fib</code> the
recursive case has two induction hypotheses, one per recursive call: the two-step
induction that the definition needs, which ordinary induction on <code>Nat</code> does not
supply directly. For <code>log2</code> the recursive branch
carries an induction hypothesis for exactly the argument of the recursive call,
<code>x / 2</code>. The <code>fun_induction</code> tactic, added in Lean 4.18.0, applies it to
a goal about <code>log2 n</code>.<ref name="rel48" />

== Partial and unsafe definitions ==

Two modifiers admit definitions that are not shown to terminate, and both prevent them from
compromising proofs.<ref name="refman-rec" />

A '''<code>partial</code>''' definition is checked by the Lean kernel for type-correctness as if
recursion were allowed, and then enters the logic as an '''opaque constant''': a constant
with a type and no definition the Lean kernel may unfold. The compiler still produces ordinary
code for it.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
partial def collatz (n : Nat) : Nat :=
  if n ≤ 1 then 0 else 1 + collatz (if n % 2 = 0 then n / 2 else 3 * n + 1)

#eval collatz 27
#print collatz
</pre>

Lean prints <code>111</code> and then <code>opaque collatz : Nat → Nat</code>. Whether this
function terminates on every input is the open Collatz problem. A partial function may
appear in propositions and proofs, but its equational theory is very weak: no property of its
values that depends on its definition can be proved, because the logic sees no
definition.<ref name="refman-rec" /> Even unfolding it fails:

<pre class="lean lean-cont lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : collatz 1 = 0 := by unfold collatz; rfl
</pre>

Lean reports <code>Tactic `unfold` failed to unfold `collatz` in</code> followed by the goal,
<code>collatz 1 = 0</code>. For the same reason a partial function's result type must be shown to be inhabited.
Otherwise a partial function into <code>Empty</code> would be an opaque constant producing an
element of an empty type, and so a proof of anything:<ref name="refman-rec" />

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
partial def loop (n : Nat) : Empty := loop (n + 1)
</pre>

is rejected: <code>failed to compile 'partial' definition `loop`, could not prove that the
type Nat → Empty is nonempty</code>.

An '''<code>unsafe</code>''' definition has none of these restrictions. It may recurse freely,
its type need not be inhabited, and it may use operations, such as unchecked casts between
types, that break the equational theory. In exchange it may be used only by other
<code>unsafe</code> definitions, and never in a theorem:<ref name="refman-rec" />

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
unsafe def spin (n : Nat) : Empty := spin (n + 1)

theorem oops : False := (spin 0).elim
</pre>

Lean reports <code>(kernel) invalid declaration, it uses unsafe declaration 'spin'</code>.
The prefix shows that the refusal is made by Lean's kernel itself, so it does not depend on
the elaborator being correct.
<code>partial</code> and <code>unsafe</code> thus mark the boundary between Lean as a
programming language, where non-termination is a fact of life, and Lean as a logic, where it
would be a contradiction.
